name: İttihadism
summary: İttihadism is the program of the Committee of Union and Progress, the Young Turk organization that restored the Ottoman constitution in 1908 and ruled the empire from 1913 to 1918. It combined constitutionalism with a centralizing, state-strengthening nationalism and Ottomanism that shifted toward Islam and Turkish dominance, a protectionist national economy, and a disciplined party that repressed opponents and, in wartime, pursued the destruction of the Armenian population of Anatolia.
scope: The CUP's program and record from 1908 to 1918, taken from scholarship on the Committee (Kayali, Onsoy and Atmaca, Aslan, Bilici) and the USHMM account of its wartime policy, with its 1908 programme clauses and 1913 party regulations as primary texts. It covers the early constitutionalist phase, the post-1913 consolidation and the wartime government; it does not include Turkish nationalism or Pan-Turkism as wider movements, the Liberty and Entente decentralists, or the Kemalist republic. Because the record changed from secular Ottomanism toward Islamism and Turkish dominance, answers rest on the mature record in power.

decide-locally.rationale: The Unionists subscribed to a program of centralization and opposed administrative autonomy for the provinces; scholars treat centralization as the movement's central project, and the 1913 Provincial Law's decentralizing clauses were a concession under pressure.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Preserving the empire's territorial integrity was the CUP's pressing concern from 1908, and its 1913 coup at the Sublime Porte was staged to stop the government surrendering besieged Edirne; centralization was justified by that aim.

right-to-secede.rationale: The movement upheld the imperial polity against separatism and denounced decentralization, so a regional right to secede contradicts its stated aim of keeping all Ottoman lands together.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Kayali records the CUP as opposed in principle to extending local autonomy to provinces and as inflexible toward the demands of the religious minorities and the Arab, Albanian and Armenian autonomists.

communal-electorates.rationale: The CUP's Ottomanism denied political representation on a religious-communal basis, which is why critics charged it with Turkification.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Article 3 of the 1913 internal regulations makes majority decisions binding on every member, and article 13 forbids members to criticize party decisions outside the meeting hall.

suppress-opposition.rationale: In power the Unionists used manipulation, intimidation and violence in the 1912 'big-stick' election, closed the Beirut Reform Club, dissolved unions by the 1909 Strike Law and suppressed Arab opposition on the eve of the war.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The 1909 Strike Law banned unions in public-service establishments, dissolved existing unions and imposed prison terms for inciting stoppages, while scholars dispute whether it prohibited strikes outright.

unions-good.rationale: The CUP government's 1909 Strike Law dissolved the unions then existing, workers' and employers' alike, and forbade new ones in public services, a record of curbing rather than welcoming unions.

political-violence-never.rationale: The CUP took power at gunpoint in the 1913 Sublime Porte raid, used violence in the 1912 elections and, per Onsoy and Atmaca, assassination and other violent methods to establish control.

revolution-justified.rationale: The 1908 Revolution that restored the constitution was carried out by the CUP's Macedonian officer branches, and the movement repeated forcible seizure in January 1913.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The CUP used martial-law and emergency measures after 1909 and during the Italian war, and the wartime government used the military emergency to carry out deportations and its population policy.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Ottomanism rested on loyalty to the dynasty; the CUP curbed the sultan's constitutional prerogatives and deposed Abdulhamid in 1909 but installed his brother and kept the dynasty.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The CUP annulled the 1876 clause giving the sultan power to dissolve Parliament in 1908, but in 1912 tried to restore it to manipulate Parliament, and from 1914 Central Committee decisions replaced legislation.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: The CUP struck the sultan's dissolution power from the constitution in 1908 and then tried in 1912 to restore it, while in 1912 it pressed Sultan Resad to dissolve Parliament, so its record points both ways.

single-official-language.rationale: The 1908 programme made Turkish the state language and compulsory in primary schools, yet Kayali finds Arabic stayed in the press, primary schooling and religion, and the stricter enforcement was repealed in places.

minority-language-support.rationale: Unionist governments resisted language demands as a threat to unity, then in 1913-14 conceded Arabic in provincial administration and schools to the Arab Congress, so the record points both ways.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The wartime CUP government pursued a long-term population policy to strengthen Muslim Turkish elements in Anatolia, but Kayali finds it upheld a multiethnic imperial polity and did not carry out a Turkish nationalist programme.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: The USHMM records that the CUP government deported and destroyed the Armenian population of eastern Anatolia to establish Turkish Muslim dominance, though the deportations were within the empire rather than out of it.

population-transfer.rationale: The CUP government justified wartime deportations of Armenians as a security measure against a minority seen as hostile, but they were carried out inside the empire's territory and ended in mass death rather than expulsion abroad.

national-self-determination.rationale: The movement refused autonomy or separate statehood to the Albanian, Arab and Armenian movements in favor of one imperial state.

religious-nation.rationale: After 1913 the CUP redefined Ottomanism to stress Islam as its main underpinning, though it began with secular Ottomanism that placed all peoples on an equal footing.

more-religion-public.rationale: Kayali shows Unionists relying on religion for centralization and social harmony, with Islamic propaganda since 1913 and the call for jihad in 1914.

separate-church-state.rationale: Onsoy and Atmaca find Unionist reforms had secularist features, while Kayali shows the party turning to Islam as the ideological basis of the state.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: After abolishing the capitulations the CUP government raised customs tariffs and adopted a protectionist national-economy policy meant to build a Turkish Muslim bourgeoisie.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Bilici lists statism and planned, balanced development among the principles of the 1910-1918 development policy, with state-founded companies and an industry encouragement law.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The Millî Iktisat program aimed to create a Turkish Muslim bourgeoisie, and the wartime government confiscated Armenian property to finance Turkification.

free-trade.rationale: The CUP followed liberal economic policies in 1908-1913 and a protectionist national-economy line in 1913-1918, so its record points both ways.

conscription.rationale: The CUP governments drew recruits from the provinces for the Balkan and world wars and tried, but failed, to extend conscription to the Hijaz.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The government signed a secret treaty with Germany in August 1914 and joined the Central Powers in the war.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: The Unionist leadership entered a treaty of alliance with Germany in 1914, taken by a small circle of Committee leaders.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Unionist government bound itself to the German alliance during the war rather than ending alliances.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Unionist officers politicized the army after 1909 and the CUP stormed the government in 1913, but early moves sought to keep officers out of politics and Kayali disputes treating it as a military regime.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The CUP seized power in 1913 to stop the cession of Edirne but its government ended the Italian war by giving up Libya in 1912.
